headline: Slack caps Slackbot at 15 messages per user a week on Business+ and posts a $45 Enterprise+ price
tldr: Slack's $15-a-seat Business+ plan now limits its Slackbot AI agent to 15 messages per user each week. Unlimited Slackbot is an Enterprise+ feature, now listed at $45 per user a month.
who: Teams on Slack Business+ that lean on Slackbot for answers and channel summaries, and companies weighing an upgrade to Enterprise+
seo_title: Slack Business+ Slackbot limit: 15 messages per user a week (Nov 11, 2026)
seo_desc: Slack's pricing page now caps Slackbot on Business+ at 15 messages per user each week, makes unlimited Slackbot an Enterprise+ feature, and lists Enterprise+ at $45 per user a month billed annually.

redline.before: Your personal AI agent that understands conversations, files, and projects in Slack. Plan limits apply.
redline.after: Find answers, summarize channels, and work across your apps. 15 messages per user each week. Contact sales to add more.
redline.label: Pricing · Business+ · Slackbot
redline.note: A vague "plan limits apply" becomes a hard number: 15 messages per person per week.

redline.after: $45 USD per user / month, when paying annually
redline.label: Pricing · Enterprise+
redline.note: Enterprise+ gets a public list price for the first time on this page.

redline.before: Your personal AI agent that understands conversations, files, and projects in Slack. Plan limits apply.
redline.after: Find answers, summarize channels, and work across your apps. It’s unlimited for your whole team.
redline.label: Pricing · Enterprise+ · Slackbot
redline.note: Unlimited Slackbot is now the selling point of the $45 tier.

actions: If your team is on Business+, check how many Slackbot messages people actually send in a week before the 15-message cap bites
Ask Slack sales what extra Slackbot messages cost before committing to a renewal, since the page says to contact sales to add more
Compare Business+ at $15 per user a month (billed annually) with Enterprise+ at $45 if unlimited Slackbot matters to you
what:
Slack's pricing page changed overnight in two ways that matter for anyone paying for its AI features.

## Change 1: Slackbot gets a weekly cap on Business+

On Nov 10, the Business+ plan described Slackbot as "Your personal AI agent that understands conversations, files, and projects in Slack. Plan limits apply." On Nov 11 the same row reads: "Find answers, summarize channels, and work across your apps. 15 messages per user each week. Contact sales to add more." Business+ is listed at $15 per user a month billed annually, or $18 billed monthly. The feature is also renamed from "Slackbot (personal AI agent)" to plain "Slackbot" across the plan table, and the comparison table adds "Consumption based" and "Usage limits" rows.

## Change 2: Enterprise+ gets a price, and unlimited Slackbot

Enterprise+ used to say "Contact sales for pricing." It now shows "$45 USD per user / month, when paying annually," still with a Contact Sales button. Its Slackbot row now reads "Unlimited Slackbot" with "It’s unlimited for your whole team."

What stays the same: The note that Business+ customers on Salesforce invoice plans can unlock higher message limits by buying Flex Credits through Salesforce is unchanged apart from formatting. Pro still lists Slackbot without a stated number.

What you can do: Business+ admins should check how heavily their teams use Slackbot; 15 messages a week is about three a workday.

headline: Microsoft 365 runs a 30%-off first term on Personal and Premium
tldr: Microsoft is offering 30% off the first year or first month of Microsoft 365 Personal ($69.99 instead of $99.99 a year) and Premium ($139.99 instead of $199.99). Both renew at full price.
who: People buying a new Microsoft 365 Personal or Premium subscription

redline.after: Limited-time offer Microsoft 365 Personal $9.99 $6.99/first month $99.99 $69.99/first year
redline.label: Pricing · Microsoft 365 Personal
redline.note: The discount covers only the first month or first year.

redline.before: Subscription automatically renews at the regular price and selected term, unless cancelled in Microsoft account.
redline.after: Limited-time offer and 1 month trial cannot be combined. Subscription automatically renews at the regular price unless cancelled in Microsoft account.
redline.label: Pricing · Fine print
redline.note: You can take the discount or the free month, not both.

actions: Set a reminder before your first year ends: Personal renews at $99.99 and Premium at $199.99
Pick either the 30% offer or the one-month free trial; the page says they can't be combined
what:
Microsoft's compare-plans page now leads with a "Limited-time offer": "Save 30% and get more from Microsoft 365." Microsoft 365 Personal shows $6.99 for the first month (regularly $9.99) or $69.99 for the first year (regularly $99.99). Microsoft 365 Premium shows $13.99 for the first month (regularly $19.99) or $139.99 for the first year (regularly $199.99). Family is not part of the offer and stays at $12.99 a month or $129.99 a year.

The fine print now says: "Limited-time offer and 1 month trial cannot be combined. Subscription automatically renews at the regular price unless cancelled in Microsoft account." The page no longer shows the "Save up to 17% when you pay yearly" banner. It gives no end date for the offer.

who: Claude subscribers and Team or Enterprise buyers comparing which apps each plan includes

what:
Anthropic's pricing page changed its feature lists without changing any prices. "Claude Dashboards (beta)" is now "Claude Data" without a beta tag, and two new rows marked "New" appear: "Claude Sheets (beta)" and "Claude Whiteboards (beta)." headline: Dave & Buster's new privacy policy says it sells your data to data brokers and lists CCTV video and keystroke tracking
tldr: Dave & Buster's replaced its 2020 privacy notice on Nov 4. The old one opened with "We do not sell"; the new one says it sells or shares data with ad networks and data brokers, and adds CCTV video and ID details.
who: Anyone who uses daveandbusters.com or the Dave & Buster's app, plays with a Power Card, is in the D&B Rewards program, or visits a Dave & Buster's location.
seo_title: Dave & Buster's privacy policy (Nov 4, 2026): sells data to data brokers, CCTV video, keystroke tracking
seo_desc: Dave & Buster's replaced its 2020 privacy notice on November 4, 2026. It now says it sells or shares data with ad networks and data brokers, records CCTV video and lets tools capture keystrokes. What changed and how to opt out.

redline.before: We do not sell or otherwise share personal information about you, except as described in this Privacy Notice.
redline.after: We sell or share this information with advertising networks, data brokers and other companies involved in digital advertising to assist us in delivering personalized ads to you.
redline.label: Privacy Policy · Selling and sharing
redline.note: The old notice led with a no-sale promise (with a California caveat further down). The new one names data brokers as buyers.

redline.after: This may include tools that capture your keystrokes, mouse clicks, screen touches, and information about when, how and from where you accessed our Sites.
redline.label: Privacy Policy · Cookies and Other Tracking Technologies
redline.note: Third parties on the site may record what you type, click and tap.

redline.after: Video of you captured on CCTV security cameras installed in our locations.
redline.label: Privacy Policy · Information We Collect (Audio and visual information)
redline.note: In-store camera footage and ID details are now listed as personal information D&B collects.

actions: Opt out of the sale and sharing of your data with Dave & Buster's online form (the "Your Privacy Choices" link at the bottom of daveandbusters.com), or email guest.relations@daveandbusters.com or call 1-888-300-1515
Turn on Global Privacy Control in each browser you use; D&B says it honors the signal per browser, only in states with privacy laws that apply to it
If you're in D&B Rewards and want out, call (844) 515-5157, the number the policy gives for leaving the program
what:
Dave & Buster's posted a new privacy policy marked "Effective Date: November 4, 2026". It replaces a notice marked "Effective Date: January 1, 2020", which was still live when the Wayback Machine captured the page on October 15, 2026. We compared that capture with the live page on November 11, 2026. This is a full rewrite, not a few edits. It now covers the website, the app, and anyone who will "play games or enjoy other digital experiences at our locations", which means the arcade floor as well as the website.

## Change 1: from "We do not sell" to naming data brokers

The 2020 notice's sharing section began: "We do not sell or otherwise share personal information about you, except as described in this Privacy Notice." Its California section did say that ad partners' access "may be considered a sale under CCPA under certain circumstances" and that D&B "engages in online advertising practices that may potentially be considered 'sales' under the CCPA." The new policy states it outright: "We sell or share this information with advertising networks, data brokers and other companies involved in digital advertising to assist us in delivering personalized ads to you." The data in question is "personal identifiers (including email address; phone number; and unique identifier) and internet or other electronic activity information." The policy says this happens "by allowing third parties to place cookies or other tracking technologies on our website" and "by sharing information with our advertising partners." It lists "Advertising companies and data brokers" as the third parties that receive personal information, and "advertising companies and data brokers" among the places D&B gets information from. (The 2020 notice already listed "Third-party data resellers" as a source.)

## Change 2: tools that capture keystrokes

A new cookies section says D&B lets third parties use tracking tools "so that they can provide analytics information and deliver targeted ads tailored to you", and that "This may include tools that capture your keystrokes, mouse clicks, screen touches, and information about when, how and from where you accessed our Sites." It names one tool: "Among other tools, we use Google Ads." The 2020 notice didn't mention keystrokes. It only said data "might be collected by us or 3rd parties, such as Smartlook.com, s.r.o.", without saying what that company collects.

## Change 3: CCTV video, IDs and in-store data

The list of what D&B collects now includes "Video of you captured on CCTV security cameras installed in our locations", "drivers' license or other identification card information", "status as a first responder", "Power Card and Rewards accounts information and balances", and "information collected electronically from you in our stores." The 2020 notice mentioned Power Card purchases but none of the others. The policy says it has "collected these same categories of personal information in the 12 months before the date of this Policy", so this describes what D&B was already doing, not only what it plans to do. It also lists "Inferences drawn from personal information", and says D&B has disclosed "video of you captured on CCTV security cameras" for business purposes in the past 12 months, without saying to whom.

## What D&B says your data is worth

The policy adds a "Notice of Financial Incentive" for the Dave & Buster's Rewards program. It says D&B collects "your name and phone number and track your associated purchases so we can send you personalized offers". Then it puts a price on it: "We estimate the value of personal information as less than a dollar, based upon the value of bonus Game Chips."

## What got better

Some of the changes help you. Opt-outs must be honored "no later than 15 business days after receipt of your request", down from "no later than 45 days" in the 2020 notice. D&B now says "We recognize the Global Privacy Control signal when sent from IP addresses in states with privacy laws that apply to us", although only "for that browser only". It says that "if we know you are under the age of 18, we won't knowingly sell or share your personal information for targeted advertising". The 2020 notice only promised not to knowingly sell the data of children under 13. The policy now lists rights for residents of 17 states, and says rights for Alabama, Louisiana and Oklahoma residents come when those laws take effect in 2027.

## Odd details

The SMS section ends: "You can also reach us at privacy@mainevent.com." Main Event is the family-entertainment chain Dave & Buster's has owned since 2022 (Wikipedia). Main Event's own privacy policy, "Effective January 1, 2026", doesn't contain the data-broker, CCTV or keystroke language. D&B also says "We do not respond to the DNT or 'Do Not Track' signal."

## Why this matters now

In October 2025, two California residents filed a proposed class action in federal court in the Northern District of California. They allege that daveandbusters.com kept sending browsing data to Meta, Google, TikTok, Microsoft and X after visitors clicked "Reject All" on the cookie banner (National Law Review, October 30, 2025). These are allegations, not findings. The new policy describes in much more detail the tracking that suit is about.

Coverage (checked Nov 11, 2026): we found no news coverage of the November 4 policy. Search results show only the policy itself.
faq: When did Dave & Buster's change its privacy policy?
The new policy is marked "Effective Date: November 4, 2026". It replaced a notice dated January 1, 2020, which was still on the site in an October 15, 2026 Wayback Machine capture.
Does Dave & Buster's sell my data?

Its policy now says so. It says D&B may "sell" (as some state laws define it) personal identifiers such as email, phone number and a unique identifier, plus internet activity, and that it shares them "with advertising networks, data brokers and other companies involved in digital advertising". It says it doesn't sell or share other categories this way.
How do I opt out of Dave & Buster's selling my data?

Use the opt-out form linked from "Your Privacy Choices" at the bottom of daveandbusters.com, email guest.relations@daveandbusters.com, or call 1-888-300-1515. D&B also honors the Global Privacy Control signal, per browser, from states with privacy laws that apply to it. It says it will act on opt-outs within 15 business days.
Does Dave & Buster's record video of customers?

The policy lists "Video of you captured on CCTV security cameras installed in our locations" as personal information it collects. It also says it disclosed CCTV video for business purposes in the past 12 months.
What does Dave & Buster's say my data is worth?
In its Rewards program notice: "We estimate the value of personal information as less than a dollar, based upon the value of bonus Game Chips."
Does the website record my keystrokes?

The policy says third-party tools on its sites "may include tools that capture your keystrokes, mouse clicks, screen touches, and information about when, how and from where you accessed our Sites." It doesn't say which tools or which pages.
sources: Dave & Buster's Privacy Notice (effective Jan 1, 2020), Wayback Machine capture Oct 15, 2026
Dave & Buster's Rewards Program Official Rules
National Law Review: CIPA class action complaint filed against Dave & Buster's (Oct 30, 2025)

headline: Chase bars external AI and data aggregators from using your login, and may require the mobile app and a Trusted Device from Jan 1, 2027
tldr: Chase bars external AI and aggregators from using your login, and says to change a shared password. From Jan 1, 2027, it may require the mobile app and a Trusted Device.
who: Anyone who uses Chase Online, Chase Mobile, Chase Business Online, Chase Point of Sale, J.P. Morgan Online or J.P. Morgan Mobile — especially customers who have given a budgeting app, data aggregator or AI assistant their login.
seo_title: Chase Digital Services Agreement (Oct 2026): External AI login bar, Trusted Device from Jan 1, 2027
seo_desc: Chase's Digital Services Agreement, last updated October 2026, bars External AI, automated tools and data aggregators from using your login (effective Oct 27). From Jan 1, 2027, it may require the Chase mobile app and a Trusted Device, or deny access.

redline.before: If you permit any other person or entity, including any data aggregation service providers, to use the Digital Platforms or to access or use your Card numbers, account numbers, PINs, user IDs, Passwords, or other means to access your accounts, you are responsible for any transactions and activities performed from your accounts
redline.after: Third parties — including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators — are prohibited from using your Login Credentials to access the Digital Platforms or your accounts or Services thereon.
redline.label: Digital Services Agreement · sharing credentials (Wayback Feb 19, 2022 capture, last updated 4/1/2021, vs. October 2026 text)
redline.note: The 2021 wording made you responsible if you let an aggregator in. The October 2026 wording forbids External AI, automated tools and aggregators from using your login.

redline.after: If you have shared your Login Credentials with any third party, you must change those credentials to ensure that the third party can no longer use them or access your information through the Digital Platforms.
redline.label: Digital Services Agreement · key changes cover and sharing section (effective October 27, 2026)
redline.note: If you already gave a budgeting app or AI tool your password, Chase says you have to change it.

redline.after: Effective January 1, 2027, we may require you to (i) download and use our mobile application, and (ii) use a Trusted Device, as defined in this agreement to verify your identity. Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law.
redline.label: Digital Services Agreement · key changes cover (last updated October 2026)
redline.note: This January 1, 2027 date is in the cover summary. The body section "Authentication via Trusted Device" has the same may-require and may-deny language, without that date.

actions: If you have shared your Chase login with any third party (an AI tool, a budgeting app, an aggregator), change that password, as the October 2026 agreement requires
Before January 1, 2027, install the Chase Mobile app on a smartphone you control and only you use; Chase may deny access to online banking until you do, unless an accommodation is required by law
Don't give your Chase username and password to an AI agent or aggregator; the agreement says third-party access is permitted through approved APIs with your authorization
what:
Chase's Digital Services Agreement, the contract for Chase Online, Chase Mobile, Chase Business Online, Chase Point of Sale, J.P. Morgan Online and J.P. Morgan Mobile, was last updated October 2026. We fetched the current PDF at static.chasecdn.com (dsa1_la.pdf) on November 11, 2026. A longer related PDF at the same library (dsa_la.pdf) is last updated November 2026 and opens with the same two dated changes, plus new Zelle Brokerage terms; the quotes below are from dsa1_la.pdf unless noted.

The October 2026 PDF opens with a "We're making key changes" cover. Two dates matter.

## Change 1: External AI, automated tools and data aggregators may not use your login (effective October 27, 2026)

The cover says: "Effective October 27, 2026, we have made changes to ratify your obligation to not share credentials with third parties and that third parties — including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators — are prohibited from using your Login Credentials to access the Digital Platforms or your accounts or Services thereon. We permit third-party applications and tools, including External AI, to access customer account data through approved application programming interfaces ("APIs") with your authorization."

The same paragraph continues: "If you have shared your Login Credentials with any third party, you must change those credentials to ensure that the third party can no longer use them or access your information through the Digital Platforms."

That wording is repeated in the body under "Sharing Your Login Credentials with Third Parties is Prohibited." The definitions section says "External AI: means, collectively, Third-party AI and Third-party AI Agent, and includes any provider thereof." A "Third-party AI Agent" includes "any AI-based software or service provided by a third party that takes autonomous, semi-autonomous, or non-autonomous action on behalf of, or at the instruction of, any person (human or entity), including you." "Login Credentials" are "PINs, user IDs, passwords, biometrics, security keys, syncable authenticators (e.g., passkeys), or any other means of accessing the Digital Platforms or your accounts or Services thereon."

If you still let a third party, "including External AI," access the platforms or your accounts, a long "Consequences" list says you "expressly authorize that third party to transact in your account," that Chase will "rely on, and treat as evidence of your authorization, any actions taken or instructions given by the third party as if you personally took or gave those actions or instructions," and that you "assume all risks and losses associated with such access or use." Chase also "reserve[s] the right to deny, decline, suspend, or terminate your access to the Digital Platforms, your accounts, or Services — including access facilitated by External AI or other third party — or to close your account(s), at any time, in our sole discretion and without notice. This may render External AI or your account(s) non-functional."

What it replaces (Wayback, fetched November 11, 2026): the Internet Archive has two captures of this same dsa1_la.pdf URL, from December 30, 2020 and February 19, 2022. We fetched the February 19, 2022 file. It is last updated 4/1/2021. Its "Passwords & Other Sensitive Information" section says you agree "to protect and keep confidential your Card number, account number, PIN, user ID, Password, or other means of accessing your accounts via the Digital Platforms." It also says: "If you permit any other person or entity, including any data aggregation service providers, to use the Digital Platforms or to access or use your Card numbers, account numbers, PINs, user IDs, Passwords, or other means to access your accounts, you are responsible for any transactions and activities performed from your accounts and for any use of your personal and account information by any person or entity to whom they may provide that personal and account information." There is no "External AI" definition, no ban on automated tools using your login, no instruction to change a password you have already shared, and no Trusted Device section. We could not retrieve a later pre-October 2026 capture of the related dsa_la.pdf from the Wayback Machine in this session (the archive listed captures through September 26, 2026, but returned HTTP 429). Intermediate versions may exist; the comparison above is to the 2022 capture of this same filename.

## Change 2: From January 1, 2027, Chase may require the mobile app and a Trusted Device, and may deny access until you comply

The cover says: "Effective January 1, 2027, we may require you to (i) download and use our mobile application, and (ii) use a Trusted Device, as defined in this agreement to verify your identity. Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law."

The body section "Authentication via Trusted Device" repeats the may-require and may-deny language but does not repeat the January 1, 2027 date: "To help protect your account from fraud and unauthorized access, we may require you to download and use our mobile application, and use a Trusted Device, as defined in this Agreement, to verify your identity. Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law. You should use only your personal device – one you control and only you use – as your Trusted Device. If you lose access to your Trusted Device (for example, if it is lost or stolen), you may need to verify a new one via Trusted Device Enrollment, as defined in this Agreement, which could temporarily delay your ability to access our Digital Platforms, accounts, or complete transactions and other banking activities."

A Trusted Device is defined as "A smartphone that (1) runs a Supported Mobile Operating System, and (2) we recognize as your trusted device after you use our mobile applications (for example, the Chase Mobile® app) and meet our security requirements, which we may modify from time to time in our sole discretion." Trusted Device Enrollment "may include specific identity verification and authentication methods (for example, taking a photo of an acceptable form of identification with your smartphone camera)."

Chase's customer FAQ (chase.com/personal/banking/education/basics/trusteddevice, fetched November 11, 2026) matches that definition: "A trusted device is a smartphone that you’ve verified with the Chase Mobile app in accordance with requirements established by Chase." It also says: "Currently, only smartphones with the Chase Mobile app installed and a supported operating system (such as iOS 16.0 or later or Android 11 or later) can be trusted devices. Tablets, laptops, desktop computers, and iPads are not eligible at this time." And: "For your security, only use your own device to access your Chase account, and don't enroll a device you share." The FAQ does not mention the January 1, 2027 date.

What you can do: if you have given your Chase password to an app, an aggregator or an AI assistant, change it. Before January 1, 2027, if you want to keep using Chase in a browser, be ready to enroll a personal smartphone in the Chase Mobile app; the agreement says Chase may deny access until you do, unless the law requires an accommodation. If you only have a tablet, laptop or shared phone, the FAQ says those are not eligible as Trusted Devices.

Coverage (checked November 11, 2026): a November 4 Hunton Andrews Kurth alert in the National Law Review, "Major banks move to block or limit customer-directed AI agents," discusses Chase alongside Schwab, Citi and Wells Fargo. Its table dates Chase's action to an October 13, 2026 earnings-call remark by Jamie Dimon and describes "an updated Digital Services Agreement (effective Jan. 1, 2027)" as providing that a customer who gives an AI agent access "authorizes everything that AI agent does." The October 2026 PDF we fetched dates the External AI and credential-sharing rules to October 27, 2026, and uses January 1, 2027 for the Trusted Device and mobile-app requirement. The "authorizes everything" consequences are in the current PDF body, not only as a January 1 term. We did not find a consumer news story that quotes the October 27 External AI bar or the "you must change those credentials" line.
faq: Can a budgeting app or AI assistant still log in to my Chase account with my password?

Not under the October 2026 agreement. From October 27, 2026, "third parties — including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators — are prohibited from using your Login Credentials" to access Chase's digital platforms or your accounts. Chase says third-party apps, including External AI, may access account data "through approved application programming interfaces ("APIs") with your authorization."
I already shared my Chase password with an app. What does the agreement say I should do?

Change it. The agreement says: "If you have shared your Login Credentials with any third party, you must change those credentials to ensure that the third party can no longer use them or access your information through the Digital Platforms."
When might Chase require the mobile app and a Trusted Device?

The cover of the October 2026 Digital Services Agreement says: "Effective January 1, 2027, we may require you to (i) download and use our mobile application, and (ii) use a Trusted Device… Until you do, we may deny access to our Digital Platforms, the Services, and your accounts, unless an accommodation is required by law." It is a "may require," not a promise that every customer will be locked out on that date.
What counts as a Trusted Device?

The agreement defines it as a smartphone that runs a supported mobile operating system and that Chase recognizes after you use its mobile apps and meet its security requirements. Chase's FAQ (fetched November 11, 2026) says only smartphones with the Chase Mobile app and a supported OS (it gives iOS 16.0 or later or Android 11 or later as examples) can be trusted devices, and that tablets, laptops, desktop computers and iPads are not eligible at this time. It also says to use your own device and not to enroll a device you share.
Is this the same as Wells Fargo's Nov 24 AI-agent terms?

No. Wells Fargo's upcoming Online Access Agreement (effective November 24, 2026) lets AI agents be used but puts the risk on the customer. Chase's October 2026 agreement prohibits External AI, automated tools and data aggregators from using your login credentials, points them to approved APIs, and, from January 1, 2027, may require the mobile app and a Trusted Device.
